topic: membership inference; privacy-risk measurement; subgroup privacy
status: bounded cross-paper measurement gap; global novelty unconfirmed
claim: In the audited evidence, record-level membership-risk scores are validated against particular attacks and populations, not against a known optimal attacker or a universal privacy ground truth. In the 2017 DTP study, the per-record correlation between PDTP and attack success ranges from 0.4864 to 0.7653 across three attacks on Purchase data, and one record at baseline under the distance attack reaches 0.94 under the untargeted attack; the maximum-over-three-attacks association rises to 0.8936. A later SHAPr paper evaluates ten datasets but explicitly notes that, without a demonstrably optimal MIA, metric effectiveness can only be evaluated against specific available attacks. Other selected work reports subgroup vulnerability above aggregate rates. The evidence supports evaluating attack coverage and subgroup tails alongside an average risk score, not discarding such metrics.
positive_evidence: Long et al. report attack-specific PDTP correlations of 0.4864, 0.5052, and 0.7653 for three attacks on NN-Purchase; correlation with maximum per-target attack accuracy is 0.8936. One example has baseline distance-attack accuracy but 0.94 untargeted-attack accuracy.
The DTP paper provides formal definitions and proves conditional relations under training-stability assumptions; the finding does not refute those theorems.

SHAPr evaluates score susceptibility over ten datasets with modified-entropy and likelihood-ratio attacks. Its recall table shows strong performance against likelihood-ratio attacks, while results against the less effective attack vary by dataset and sometimes favor SPRS.

A 2019 study reports aggregate membership attack accuracy 70.14% versus 89.90% for its racial-minority image subgroup on one LFW setup; its Adult/CIFAR experiments also vary subgroup vulnerability with representation.
counterevidence: PDTP’s association with the maximum of three attacks is strong in the reported Purchase experiment; one counterexample does not establish pervasive failure.

SHAPr broadens evaluation to ten datasets and multiple attacks and reports high recall in many settings; this is substantive counterevidence to a claim that existing metrics have no cross-dataset value.
The 2019 subgroup results are tied to selected datasets, models, attack setup, and group definitions; reported attack accuracy is not a universal population risk estimate.

The 2016 On-Average KL-Privacy paper is theoretical for a specified class of mechanisms; average-case and worst-case guarantees answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable metrics.

sources.sections: formal distribution-dependent definition and stated Gibbs/max-entropy mechanism results; two illustrative simulations

falsifiable_test: Pre-register one matched benchmark spanning at least ten datasets with explicit rare/sensitive subgroups, several model families, and a suite of black-box and white-box membership attacks (including adaptive attacks). Compare DTP/PDTP, SHAPr, generalization-based signals, and subgroup-specific summaries against per-record attack outcomes. Report per-attack calibration, false-negative rate at fixed false-positive rates, worst-subgroup and upper-tail recall, attack-to-attack rank stability, utility, and metric computation cost. Repeat under controlled class imbalance and train/test distribution shifts. The lead weakens if risk rankings remain calibrated and stable across attack families, subgroup strata, and shifts, with negligible additional false negatives from stronger attacks.
limitations: This is a synthesis of a fixed six-record security/privacy cell plus two targeted arXiv follow-ups; the cell is heterogeneous and only some records directly concern ML membership inference. The SHAPr study is not a proof of optimal-attacker coverage, and the subgroup study does not establish population-wide disparity. No new attacks or independent reproduction were run; novelty is unconfirmed.

topic: smart grids; differential privacy; demand-response optimization
status: bounded simulation result and external-validation opportunity; global novelty unconfirmed
claim: For one centralized event-based demand-response formulation, the audited paper’s Laplace-based simulations show that the utility-optimality cost of privacy depends strongly on customer count, customer mix, demand/utility correlation, and whether privacy levels can vary by customer. Reported costs range from about 0.59 to 0.63 in one 500-customer mixed setting and approach 1 in some homogeneous-privacy scenarios, while a variable-privacy scenario is around 0.4. These are scenario-specific simulated outcomes, not a universal cost of differential privacy or a field estimate.
positive_evidence: The study varies customer type, utility-demand correlation, privacy level, customer count, and generation capacity in a 4-bus Canadian-benchmark feeder model, with up to 1,500 simulated customers.

It derives an analytic bound and complements it with repeated numerical optimization; reported trends show stronger privacy (lower ε) can increase objective loss and mixed-customer scenarios can differ from residential-only scenarios.
Allowing heterogeneous privacy settings reduces the reported cost in the studied variable-capacity scenario, suggesting a concrete control variable for follow-up tests.
counterevidence: The evaluation is on simulated feeder/customer data, not a utility deployment or field demand-response trace.

The exact cost depends on the paper’s objective, feeder, demand/utility generation, Laplace mechanism, and definition of privacy cost; it is not directly transferable to other mechanisms or grid configurations.
The paper provides positive within-model evidence for a privacy/optimality tradeoff; the finding concerns transfer and sensitivity, not that the proposed mechanism is ineffective.

sources.title: Assessing the Privacy Cost in Centralized Event-Based Demand Response for Microgrids
sources.sections: §V simulation setup and case studies; Figures 2–5 and results discussion; §VI conclusion

falsifiable_test: Replay the mechanism on versioned operational or realistic synthetic traces from multiple feeder topologies, with a preregistered range of participation, customer mix, generation uncertainty, privacy budgets, and mechanisms. Compare homogeneous and personalized ε at matched formal privacy accounting; report objective loss, constraint violations, customer-level utility, runtime, and uncertainty across days/feeders. The transfer concern weakens if the published cost curves and personalized-privacy advantage replicate across held-out feeders and measured traces.
limitations: One historical arXiv paper and one simulated feeder family; no independent replication or operational dataset was reviewed. The reported numerical values are not comparable to papers using different objective functions or privacy definitions.

topic: vehicular security; pseudonym credential infrastructure; privacy systems
status: bounded systems result; deployment transfer unverified
claim: The 2016 VPKI paper provides a full implementation and a controlled 10,000-emulated-client evaluation, reporting about 500 ms to obtain 100 pseudonyms and resilience to one measured PCA crash. However, its testbed explicitly removes network propagation delay and excludes vehicle-side key generation from the reported provisioning time. The reported speedup therefore supports the implementation under its matched lab setup, while end-to-end deployment latency and realistic network/load scalability remain unmeasured in this paper.
positive_evidence: The paper reports a standard-compliant C++ implementation and evaluates client/server protocol delays, revocation, DDoS load, and a PCA crash in a controlled virtualized testbed.
The setup emulates 10,000 vehicle clients and reports roughly 500 ms for obtaining 100 pseudonyms; the authors report a four-fold improvement over the best earlier results under similar setups.
The system addresses an honest-but-curious infrastructure and proposes policy-aligned credential lifetimes to reduce trivial timing linkage.
counterevidence: Network propagation delay is intentionally eliminated, and key-pair generation is assumed to occur offline; neither is included in the quoted provisioning time.
The paper names realistic access-network effects as future work; a VM emulator is not a field vehicular network deployment.
The fixed-lifetime anti-linkage policy trades privacy benefits against overprovisioning and contact frequency, so security and operational costs need joint measurement.

sources.title: Towards Deploying a Scalable & Robust Vehicular Identity and Credential Management Infrastructure
sources.sections: §V evaluation setup (Tables IV–V), provisioning results, failure experiment, and stated network-delay limitation

falsifiable_test: Reproduce the implementation with version-pinned software and cryptographic parameters in a network emulator or field-like trace replay. Include vehicle key generation, realistic latency/loss/mobility, credential renewal policies, server scaling, and simultaneous PCA/LTCA failures. Report tail latency, successful credential throughput, revocation delay, anonymity-set/linkability measures, resource use, and overhead under matched baselines. The deployment-transfer concern weakens if reported latency and scaling remain within predeclared service targets across held-out network/load traces.
limitations: One historical paper and one virtualized testbed; no current implementation, independent replication, or field data was evaluated. The reported four-fold speed comparison is only meaningful relative to the paper’s matched historical setup.
